spotting-the-alien-who-is-the-bar-raiser.core: In an Amazon loop, the bar raiser is usually from an unrelated org, asks deeper follow-up questions ('What exactly did you do? What would you do differently?'), probes for data and failure, and is less interested in the team's specific tech. You don't need to identify them; treat every interviewer as the bar raiser.

first_principles.problem: Candidates relax with an interviewer who seems unrelated to the team, who turns out to hold the veto.
truths: Bar raisers come from outside the team.
Any interviewer could be the one.

analogy.title: A mystery shopper
analogy.story: Any customer could be the inspector, so great service must be universal.
analogy.breaks: Mystery shoppers stay hidden; bar raisers sometimes introduce themselves.

example.title: Follow-up drill
flow: 'You said the team fixed it; what did you do?'

steps.label: Prep
steps.detail: Have three layers of detail per story.

example.outcome: ready for deep probing in any round.

check.q: What's the safest strategy if you can't tell who the bar raiser is?
check.a: Treat every interviewer as the bar raiser and give each round full, detailed effort.

the-conviction-trap.core: Hiring debriefs reward strong, specific advocacy, and lukewarm 'inclined to hire' votes often add up to no-hire. Candidates fall into the conviction trap by being merely fine everywhere. Give at least some interviewers a memorable, clear reason to champion you with standout evidence.

first_principles.problem: A candidate with no weak rounds is rejected because nobody felt strongly.
truths: Mixed-lukewarm loops are risky to approve.

analogy.title: A film that's 'pretty good' versus one critics love
analogy.story: 'Pretty good' films are forgotten; one passionate critic can launch a hit.
analogy.breaks: Films have audiences beyond critics; your loop is the whole audience.

example.title: Lukewarm vs memorable
flow: Memorable: 'I led the redesign that cut Sev-1s from 12 to 2 per quarter across 40 services'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Interviewer writes it down and advocates.

check.q: Why can a loop of 'lean hire' votes still fail?
check.a: Without a strong advocate, doubts dominate and committees default to no-hire on uncertain signal.

winning-over-the-veto-voter.core: The veto-holder looks for reasons not to hire: unclear ownership, blaming others, shallow answers or poor judgement. Win them over by owning your actions (and mistakes), going deep with data, showing learning, and staying calm and curious under challenge.

first_principles.problem: A skeptical interviewer pushes back hard and the candidate becomes defensive.

analogy.title: Being cross-examined in court
analogy.story: Calm, factual answers earn credibility; argumentative ones lose the jury.
analogy.breaks: Court is adversarial; good bar raisers want you to succeed if you meet the bar.

example.title: Handling a challenge
flow: 'Fair point: we underestimated risk. We had a 5% canary, but missed a cache dependency. I added dependency checks to the release template; zero repeats since.'

check.q: What's the best response to a pointed challenge about a past decision?
check.a: Acknowledge valid concerns, explain your reasoning with data, and describe what you learned or changed.
